topic: AutoGen to Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0: Complete Migration Walkthrough

key_points: Official Microsoft migration guide for moving AutoGen projects to the Microsoft Agent Framework Python SDK.
Frames the core shift as AutoGen's event-driven Team model moving toward Agent Framework's typed, graph-based Workflow model.

Covers side-by-side mappings for model clients, single-agent agents, sessions, streaming, tools, middleware, MCP support, agent-as-tool patterns, group chat, human-in-the-loop, checkpointing, and observability.
Highlights differences such as @tool schema inference, hosted tools, multi-turn default agent behavior, and Agent Framework's current single-process composition focus.
Announces Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 for both .NET and Python as a production-ready release with stable APIs and a long-term support commitment.
Positions Agent Framework 1.0 around enterprise multi-agent orchestration, multi-provider model support, and interoperability through MCP and A2A.
Calls out stable orchestration patterns including sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, and Magentic-One, with streaming, checkpointing, approvals, and pause/resume.

Mentions migration assistants for AutoGen and Semantic Kernel users, plus preview features such as DevUI, Foundry Hosted Agent integration, AG-UI/CopilotKit/ChatKit adapters, skills, and coding-agent harness integrations.
Repository README describes Microsoft Agent Framework as an open, multi-language framework for production-grade AI agents and multi-agent workflows in .NET and Python.

Targets teams that need orchestration beyond stateless chat, graph-based collaboration patterns, durability, restartability, observability, governance, human-in-the-loop control, and provider flexibility.
Lists key features such as Python and .NET support, multiple agent providers, middleware, samples, hosting patterns, and support for local and cloud deployment.
AutoGen repository now labels the project as in maintenance mode.
States AutoGen will not receive new features or enhancements and is community managed going forward.
Directs new users to Microsoft Agent Framework and encourages existing users to migrate through the official AutoGen to Agent Framework guide.
Positions Microsoft Agent Framework as AutoGen's enterprise-ready successor with stable APIs, long-term support, multi-agent orchestration, multi-provider support, and A2A/MCP interoperability.
Practical third-party playbook for migrating Semantic Kernel and AutoGen prototypes to Agent Framework 1.0 across .NET and Python teams.
Argues teams should treat migration as a platform re-baseline, not only a class-by-class port.
Recommends defining agent boundaries, execution contracts, approval rules, timeout/retry policies, handoff contracts, and observability baselines before moving code.
Suggests phased migration: inventory workflows, run a pilot with observability and failure testing, then scale to business-critical workflows.

stats.fact: Microsoft Agent Framework reached version 1.0 for both .NET and Python in April 2026, with Microsoft describing it as production-ready with stable APIs and a long-term support commitment.

Agent Framework 1.0 includes stable multi-agent orchestration patterns: sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, and Magentic-One; Microsoft says these support streaming, checkpointing, human-in-the-loop approvals, and pause/resume for long-running workflows.
The AutoGen GitHub repository states AutoGen is now in maintenance mode, will not receive new features or enhancements, and new users should start with Microsoft Agent Framework.

The official migration guide says Agent Framework keeps familiar basics such as agents around model clients, instructions, tools, function-style tools, token streaming, multimodal content, and async I/O, while changing orchestration toward typed graph workflows.

The official migration guide notes Agent Framework uses @tool with automatic schema inference, adds hosted tools such as code interpreter and web search, and makes Agent multi-turn by default while AutoGen AssistantAgent is single-turn unless max_tool_iterations is increased.

The Agent Framework repository describes the framework as built for production use cases requiring orchestration, durability, restartability, observability, governance, human-in-the-loop control, and provider flexibility.
PyPI lists agent-framework 1.8.1 as the latest release on June 9, 2026, indicating active Python package updates after the 1.0 release.

angles: Treat the migration as an architecture upgrade: first inventory agents, tools, group chats, runtime assumptions, and observability gaps, then port code.
Lead with a side-by-side mental model: AutoGen AssistantAgent/Team/GroupChat patterns map to Agent/AgentSession/Workflow and orchestration patterns, but not always one-to-one.
Emphasize production readiness: stable 1.0 APIs, long-term support, checkpointing, pause/resume, approval gates, middleware, and observability are the business reason to migrate.
Warn readers that multi-agent migration is the hard part; single-agent assistants are straightforward, but group chat and MagenticOne flows require workflow design.
Include a migration checklist for risky behavior changes: multi-turn default execution, tool iteration limits, state/session handling, human approval paths, retries, and provider support differences.
Differentiate by adding a phased rollout plan: spike, compatibility wrapper, pilot workflow, failure testing, observability baseline, and production cutover.
Explain how to keep AutoGen running during transition by isolating shared prompts/tools and migrating workflow-by-workflow rather than rewriting everything at once.
